b: We recently held interviews for an entry-level job opening on my team, to be supervised by me. This is a non-academic civil service job with a government agency. There are specific college degree requirements, so we ask for transcripts in advance to ensure the people we’re interviewing have the correct degree.

The problem, in my eyes: my boss and coworker (same level as me, but with much more job and supervisory experience) seem to put a lot of emphasis on (low/failing) grades, even when the transcript reflects a degree was conferred and the candidate has a relevant graduate degree and/or several years of post-college work experience.

When we were hiring for my first supervisee a couple years ago, I feel like we passed up a good candidate because they had really poor grades their final year of college, though they’d since had around 10 years of successful work experience at a sister agency, doing related work to what we were hiring for. Recently, we passed on another candidate for the same job for similarly poor grades, but who went on to earn a masters degree in a relevant field and was in the military for a few years. This second candidate has a lack of other necessary and ideal skills, so I’m not as sad about not making them our first pick.

I understand scrutinizing grades for someone right out of college with zero or minimal professional work experience. But, as I am a newish manager (I now have approximately 1.5 years of management experience, though I’ve been in my role for closer to 2.5 years), I want an outside opinion on how normal and/or useful it is to put such an emphasis on college (undergraduate) grades when a person has a graduate degree and/or many years of post-graduate work experience. Are extremely poor (Ds and/or Fs in multiple classes) grades in the middle and/or at the end of college really a red flag for a person’s entire post-college life? If so, how would you ask about this in an interview, while not eliciting excuses, personal health issues, or other personal, protected info?

Grades are helpful when someone doesn’t have much of a work history to look at yet. In that case, they’re functioning as a proxy for what you might expect the person to achieve on the job. It’s not a perfect proxy by any means, but with entry-level candidates without much job experience, you work with what you have.

But once someone has an actual work history to look at — and especially when they have a decade of work experience! — you don’t need a proxy, because you have the real thing. You don’t need to try to extrapolate from their grades to how they might perform on the job because you have much more directly related evidence of how they will perform … because they’ve been working!

Moreover, there are all sorts of reasons someone might get bad grades in school but still go on to a successful career: family or health issues that have since been resolved, immaturity as a 19-year-old that they grew out of as they moved past young adulthood (this one is very common), simply not enjoying academics and being more motivated by the work world, and on and on. The idea that someone’s academic performance as a teenager/early 20something is what they should be judged by for their rest of their lives — particularly when they have an actual work record to look at — is silly.

As for how to ask about low grades in an interview anyway, frankly I wouldn’t! If they have a substantial work record since college, their grades are irrelevant. But if you have to ask in order to get your boss and coworker to give them a chance, ask in a way that highlights their post-college success. For example: “Your grades in college weren’t strong, but you’ve excelled in your jobs since then. What’s your sense of what caused that discrepancy?”
